title: Systemd Lingering User Session Fails with "timeout" During Boot When Authenticated via SSSD | SUSE | Support Center
plain_text:
Systemd Lingering User Session Fails with "timeout" During Boot When Authenticated via SSSD
Environment
Help Environment

SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 15 SP6

Situation
This issue occurs on systems utilizing systemd and configured with the System Security Services Daemon (SSSD) for network-based authentication (such as LDAP or Active Directory), where systemd lingering has been enabled for a specific user account (e.g., via loginctl enable-linger <username>).
During system startup, a network-authenticated user configured for lingering fails to spawn a background session. The system boot process may appear to hang for approximately 90 seconds.
Checking the status of the user's systemd service (systemctl status user@<UID>.service) or reviewing the system journal (journalctl -u user@<UID>.service -b) reveals the following sequence of errors:
systemd[1]: Starting User Manager for UID 32021...
systemd[1]: user@32021.service: start operation timed out. Terminating.
systemd[1]: user@32021.service: Failed with result 'timeout'.
systemd[1]: Failed to start User Manager for UID 32021.
Resolution
Disable the SSSD systemd sockets to prevent them from handling the activation. 
# systemctl disable --now sssd-nss.socket sssd-pam.socket
Open the SSSD configuration file (/etc/sssd/sssd.conf) in a text editor.
Locate the [sssd] section. Modify the services line to explicitly include nss and pam.
For example,

Change from:
services = ifp

Change to:
services = nss, pam, ifp
Restart the SSSD service to apply the changes, or reboot the server.
# systemctl restart sssd.service
Cause
This issue is caused by a circular dependency (a deadlock) between systemd (PID 1) and SSSD's default socket activation behavior during the boot sequence.
When systemd attempts to start a lingering user session for a network user, it invokes a PAM and NSS lookup to retrieve the user's account details. When SSSD is configured for socket activation, these requests hit dormant local sockets (/var/lib/sss/pipes/nss and pam). The sockets then send a signal to systemd requesting it to wake up the sssd-nss.service and sssd-pam.service to process the request.
However, systemd is already occupied waiting for the user@<UID>.service startup process to complete. Systemd is waiting for the user session to start, the user session is waiting for SSSD to answer, and the SSSD sockets are waiting for systemd to wake them up. This deadlock persists until the default 90-second systemd timeout is reached, at which point the process is forcefully terminated.
By defining nss and pam directly in the sssd.conf file, the main SSSD daemon spawns these responders immediately upon startup. When systemd queries the user during boot, the SSSD responders are already actively listening, bypassing the socket activation deadlock entirely.
Additional Information
As an additional best practice for lingering network users, one can ensure that systemd waits for the network and user-lookup targets to be fully online before attempting to start the user session. This can be done by creating a drop-in override for the user's service. 
Edit the service configuration file
# systemctl edit user@<UID>.service

 

Add the following configuration:
[Unit]
After=sssd.service network-online.target nss-user-lookup.target
Wants=network-online.target nss-user-lookup.target
Make systemd aware of the changes
# systemctl daemon-reload
For detailed information regarding SSSD services and socket activation, please refer to the sssd.conf(5) man page.
